title: How Our Solar System Began
summary: Travel back about 4.6 billion years to watch the Sun and planets form from a cloud of gas and dust. Then explore all eight planets, meet some of their natural satellites, and finish with a short quiz.

steps.text: About four point six billion years ago, there was no Earth or Sun here. A huge cloud of gas and dust floated in space.
Gravity is a pull between things that have mass. Gravity pulled parts of this cloud closer together.
As the cloud shrank, it spun faster, like a spinning skater pulling in their arms. Watch the dust circle the middle.

sfx.prompt: soft airy whoosh circling and gently accelerating

steps.text: Most material gathered in the center. Packed closer together, it became denser and hotter. A young star was beginning to form.
The remaining gas and dust flattened into a spinning disc around the young Sun. This leftover material would help build planets.
Pause and picture the whole system. These changes took millions of years. We have sped up time and changed sizes to help you see.

scenes.title: A Star and Its Planet Builders

steps.text: The young Sun's center became hot enough for fusion. Hydrogen nuclei joined together, releasing energy. The Sun began making its own light and heat.
The Sun is a star, mostly hydrogen and helium. It holds almost all the mass in our Solar System. The bars compare how much matter there is.
In this enlarged, sped-up view, some dust grains stuck together. Growing clumps collided and joined. Over time, they became larger bodies.

sfx.prompt: deep muffled impact followed by brief debris rumble

steps.text: Near the hot young Sun, rock and metal could stay solid. These materials helped build the four rocky inner planets. This diagram is simplified.
Farther away, it was colder, so ice could join the building material. Large growing worlds collected gas. The outer planets developed in this colder region.
The Sun helped clear away gas. Asteroids and comets remained. Gravity pulls planets inward; forward motion keeps them moving around it.

ambience.prompt: faint low cosmic rumble, steady and diffuse

steps.text: Mercury, Venus, Earth, then Mars: four rocky planets, starting nearest the Sun. Planet sizes are relative; the Sun and distances are not to scale.
Mercury is the smallest planet and closest to the Sun. Its cratered ground gets very hot in sunlight and very cold during its long nights.
Venus is almost Earth's size. Its thick atmosphere traps heat, making it the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
Earth has liquid-water oceans and an atmosphere that helps support life. It is the only world where we know life exists.
Mars is red from rusty iron in surface minerals. It has huge volcanoes, deep canyons, and signs that liquid water flowed there long ago.
Similar building materials made very different worlds. Distance from the Sun and atmosphere help explain why these rocky neighbors are so different.
Beyond Mars lies the asteroid belt. Its rocky objects are far apart, not a crowded wall. Here, their separations are compressed.
Jupiter is the largest planet, eleven Earths wide. This gas giant is mostly hydrogen and helium. Its Great Red Spot is a huge storm.
Saturn is another gas giant. Its rings hold countless pieces of ice and some rock. The enlarged detail shows pieces; the rings are extremely thin.

sfx.prompt: soft airy whoosh as ring detail expands

steps.text: Uranus is an ice giant, not a snowball. Deep inside, water, ammonia and methane are under great pressure. Uranus spins almost on its side.
Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun, another ice giant. It has powerful winds. Methane helps give both ice giants their blue-green colors.
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Outer planets grew in colder regions. This view simplifies sizes, distances and speeds.

nodes.label: Evidence for an ocean beneath the ice
Methane and ethane lakes, not water

steps.text: A moon is a natural satellite, a naturally formed object orbiting another body. Planets orbit the Sun; moons orbit them. Sizes and speeds are simplified.
Earth has one Moon. Evidence suggests a large body struck young Earth. Orbiting debris gathered together to make the Moon. This shows time sped up.

sfx.prompt: deep muffled impact followed by brief debris rumble

steps.text: Mercury and Venus have no moons. Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. All four giant planets have many moons; these dots show just a few examples.
Jupiter's icy Europa has strong evidence for an ocean beneath it. Saturn's Titan has thick air and lakes of liquid methane and ethane, not water.
Some moons grew from material around young planets. Others were captured by gravity, with energy lost. Moons orbit planets as planets travel around the Sun.
What did our Solar System form from: a cloud of gas and dust, or fully grown planets? Think before answering. A cloud of gas and dust became our Solar System.
Which planet is hottest: Mercury or Venus? Think before answering. Venus is hottest because its thick atmosphere traps heat.
What does Earth's Moon orbit: Earth or Mars? Choose your answer. We have followed a journey from a cloud to a star and planets, then to worlds with moons.

correct.text: Correct! Earth's Moon orbits Earth, while Earth travels around the Sun.
